1:
Where the image came from is canvassed and settled by none. Clarke supposes vines seen on the road to Gethsemane, with the disciples remarking on them. Barnes lists the upper room, the Temple with its golden vine, and the walk to the Mount of Olives, and prefers the last. Ellicott adds more candidates, tendrils growing into the room, the vine carved on the Temple doors, vineyards by moonlight, and the cup they had just drunk; he inclines to the cup as bound up with that night's significance, then refuses to go further, since the prompt may be some incident now wholly unknown. Robertson reaches the same conclusion from the Supper, renders the phrase the vine the genuine, and notes that Israel appeared as a vine on the Maccabean coinage. Wesley simply glosses true as most excellent, comparing the true bread.

Lightfoot presses the contrast that the word carries. Israel had been the vine into which a convert was grafted, and a rabbinic commentary works the parallel out to sixteen particulars, most of them in his judgement forced. What matters is that the grafting stock changes: men are no longer planted into the Jewish religion but into Christ, which is why the disciples came to be called by a name other than Jews. Henry draws out the humility instead, that the Sun of righteousness should take so low a comparison, and that the vine has an unsightly outside as its antitype had no form nor comeliness; unfruitful trees are said to lie, but this one will not deceive those who gather from it, as the wild gourds did.

Calvin opens the only textual question here and declines to fight it, weighing whether the Greek makes Christ the plant itself or the planted ground, citing Cicero for the diminutive, and saying he will not debate it with anyone. He lays down the rule instead: in a parable one takes the general view rather than every property, and that view has three parts, that no power of doing good is ours, that having root in him we are dressed by the Father, and that the barren are removed and burnt. Barnes makes the structural point more simply, that the nourishment of every branch and tendril passes through the one stalk, and corrects the English, vine-dresser rendering the second word better than husbandman.

On the branch taken away the witnesses agree about the reference and differ about its warmth. Gill distinguishes two sorts, those with an historical faith who are in him by profession only, as whole churches bear the name without every member being in him. Clarke names the cases bluntly, Judas, the unbelieving Jews, the apostatising disciples, and those who once truly believed and made shipwreck. Ellicott warns against the common reading that makes this the unbelieving world or the Jews: Christians in name are meant, watched daily by one who reads the inner reality. Robertson traces the word for branch to a root meaning to break, notes it is used of vine shoots only here, and ends with the driest remark in the chapter, that the clause about bearing more fruit is a good test for modern church members.

The pruning turns on a pun the English loses. Barnes spells it out, that the same Greek stem gives takes away, cleanses and clean in three successive clauses; Clarke insists the second verb means pruned rather than purged and produces Horace paring his nails with a penknife to prove the usage. Ellicott renders the last phrase already are ye clean, the pronoun emphatic, set against others still to be cleansed. Lightfoot and Gill find behind it the law counting a young tree's fruit unclean for three years, the disciples having had three years of the teaching. Calvin names the instrument: the doctrine they heard is itself the vine-dresser's knife, and Wesley adds that purity and fruitfulness help each other.
4:
Ellicott reads the clauses as cause and effect: the second is a promise that cannot fail if the first is obeyed, so the union and all that follows lie within reach of the will. Clarke turns the same command into two duties, holding fast faith and a good conscience, and continually receiving power to do good. Robertson notes the aorist imperative and warns that blind complacency is a peril to the preacher, Judas gone and the rest still to be sifted. Calvin hears reassurance rather than threat, since Christ did not begin the work of salvation to leave it unfinished, and promises his Spirit will be efficacious if we do not prevent him. Lightfoot alone suggests a specific danger in view, apostasy back out of the gospel into Judaism, a plague he expected to rage in the church.

Augustine fixes on the asymmetry of the two abidings. The branches contribute nothing to the vine and draw everything from it, so both the disciples abiding in Christ and Christ abiding in them profit them and not him; and when a branch is cut off another may spring from the living root, while the severed branch cannot live apart from it. He will not soften the conclusion either, observing that the text does not say you can do little. Chrysostom presses the division of labour: the Son contributes no less than the Father, since the Father prunes while the Son keeps them in himself, and to be cast forth means simply losing the husbandman's care.

How far the denial reaches divides two of them sharply. Calvin takes it absolutely against those who concede the words and then imagine a power of their own that co-operates with grace; the branch bears no fruit of itself, so nothing is left us but what is imparted, and before we are in him we are dry and useless wood. Ellicott holds the words have often been unduly pressed, since the context limits them to the fruit-bearing of the Christian life and the New Testament plainly recognises moral power outside Christianity. Barnes stays with dependence and its practical upshot, that good works are done in proportion as the dependence is felt. Clarke reaches for parallels, quoting a scripture of the Hindoos in which the deity calls himself sacrifice, worship, fire and victim, and a line of Theophilus that God is not contained but is himself the place of all things, and asks whether such sentiments could come from any source but revelation.

Whether a real branch can be lost is the old question, and four answers stand side by side. Wesley is bluntest: a man cast out of the vineyard was in it once. Clarke agrees and refuses the evasion, since no one cuts off a branch that was never joined, and a merely seeming union could suffer only a seeming excision, which says nothing. Calvin denies that any of the elect is ever dried up and assigns the withering to hypocrites who are green for a season. Gill notices that the words are not if ye abide not, which Christ would not suppose of true disciples, and Barnes refers the case to professors who never had real connection at all.

The closing picture is filled in from several sides. Lightfoot finds its force in Ezekiel, where the Jewish commentators take the branch for the wild vine of the forest, unfruitful as the forest trees themselves and fit only for burning. Barnes points out that the word men is not in the Greek, the verb being an impersonal they, and refers the gathering to angels. Robertson makes the same grammatical observation and supplies the servants of the vine-dresser as the unnamed subject, calling the aorists timeless and the warning against presumption vivid. Ellicott would render the last clause and they burn rather than are burned, noting that the tenses look back from the final judgment.
7:
The promise about asking is guarded by everyone who touches it. Ellicott thinks the verb probably imperative, ask what ye will, and makes the abiding of the words both the means of abiding in Christ and the proof of it. Robertson calls the command astounding and immediately conditions it, since such union leaves nothing to be asked out of accord with the mind of Christ. Calvin says God lets his people hunger to train them to earnestness, and denies leave is given to frame wishes by our own fancy; what the promise covers is not riches or honours but the vital sap of the Spirit. Barnes restricts it further, as spoken to the apostles and applying to others only so far as they share their spirit, and recalls that iniquity regarded in the heart stops the ear of God. Clarke reduces it to four steps; Gill speaks of the word becoming engrafted; Wesley notes that prayers are themselves a fruit of faith.

Ellicott alone objects to how the next verse is usually construed. Taking herein of what follows forces the conjunction, which properly expresses purpose; he lets herein look back, so the sense runs, in this granting of whatever you ask my Father is glorified, in order that you may bear much fruit and become my disciples. Robertson agrees it points both ways and makes the last verb become rather than be. Chrysostom makes it an assurance: if the Father's glory is bound up with their fruitfulness, he will hardly despise his own glory. Clarke says it is the vine-dresser's honour to own vines heavily laden and Wesley calls discipleship at once the foundation and the height of Christianity.

What love is meant divides the expositors. Calvin brushes aside those who take it of the eternal love of the Father for the Son, saying they philosophise away from the subject: whoever asks how God loves him without looking through the Mediator enters a labyrinth with neither entrance nor exit, whereas in Christ we see that love as in a mirror. Ellicott makes the same correction smaller: my love means his love toward them, not theirs to him, and he prefers abide to continue. Robertson notes the emphatic possessive, the love I have for you. Barnes distinguishes kind from degree. Henry counts a fourfold love here and observes that the Son kept his place in it even when it pleased the Father to bruise him, so those God loves may despise the hatred of the world.

Whether obedience earns the love or follows it is the next split. Calvin denies it is the cause and calls it the effect, meeting the objection that this rests our security on ourselves. Gill agrees that continuance in Christ's affection does not hang on our observance, and reads the promise as fuller discoveries of a love already held. Clarke states the converse: no sense of pardoning love survives without the obedience of faith. Wesley is sharper than either, on these terms and no other. Ellicott dissolves the dispute: the condition is not arbitrary, since keeping commandments is what love necessarily does, as true between Son and Father as between us and him.

The joy at the close draws the finest images. Chrysostom likens a soul fainting near the end of its labours to a great ship foundering within sight of harbour, which gains nothing from the length of its voyage and only makes the loss heavier. Clarke takes the last word as filled to the brim, like a vessel, says it was to drive wretchedness out of the world that Christ came into it, and notes that Bishop Pearce would construe the clause as my joy in you. Ellicott identifies the joy as Christ's own, lit by the mutual love of Father and Son, and judges that those whose religion sheds no such light have learnt little of Christianity.
12:
Gill makes this the principal command, to which every duty between Christians reduces; Ellicott adds that love to God is proved by love to men, so the two great commandments are really one; Robertson notes the tense, that they are to keep on loving. Lightfoot supplies the background: the sabbath blessing over a departing course of priests asked that brotherhood, love, peace and friendship be planted among them, yet tradition had largely put the command out of use, partly through impious vows, and the maxim about hating an enemy held good in the schools. Clarke passes on an old Latin story of the aged evangelist, carried into the assemblies and saying nothing but little children, love one another; asked why he always said the same thing, he answered that it is the Lord's commandment, and doing that alone is enough.

On the measure of love the witnesses reach for examples. Barnes recalls Damon and Pythias as a rare case of a man dying for a friend, and makes the rarity the point, since Christ died for enemies who had scorned and hunted him. Robertson quotes the phrase that self-sacrifice is the high-water mark of love, and Ellicott denies any conflict with Paul on dying for the ungodly, since what is weighed here is the height of love, not the worth of its object. Calvin observes that God could have redeemed us by a word, but judged it better not to spare his own Son, and so testify what our salvation cost him. Augustine draws from the epistle that we ought in turn to lay down our lives for the brethren, and finds the sacrament in the proverb about sitting at a ruler's table, that table being the one from which we take the body and blood of him who laid down his life.

Being called friends has a condition attached, and nobody softens it. Augustine calls it great condescension, since a man cannot be even a good servant without doing his lord's commands, and the marks of a good servant are made the marks of a friend; a good servant, he concludes, can be both at once. Wesley fires the sharpest sentence in the chapter at the clause, a thunderbolt for Antinomianism, and asks who dares say God's love does not at all depend on works. Calvin denies the honour is earned by merit while keeping the condition intact, and Robertson makes the tense mean continued, not spasmodic, obedience.

Augustine also raises the one real exegetical difficulty here. How can all things heard from the Father have been made known, when a little later in the same discourse many things are still unsaid because they cannot yet be borne? His answer is that what is still to be done is spoken of as done, as the prophet wrote that they pierced his hands and feet rather than that they would.

The change of title is worked out from several sides. Origen sets the servant who has the spirit of bondage against the friend, quoting the complaint in Malachi that a master should be feared, and noting that the servant does not know the master's will. Gill refers the older condition to the legal dispensation, where children differed nothing from servants under a spirit of bondage. Barnes gives the reason: it is a condition of slavery not to be admitted to a master's counsels, while friendship's privilege is to know his plans. Ellicott notes the irony that the word refused means bond-slave, and that the foremost apostles afterwards took it as their own favourite title. Robertson makes the same point of Paul and asks whether we are friends of Christ. Lightfoot recalls that Abraham bore the name first. Calvin takes the whole as proof of love, the heart of Christ laid open in the gospel, so none need climb above the clouds or search the deep for assurance.
16:
Gill and Lightfoot both hear the saying as a deliberate reversal of Jewish practice, where a disciple picked his own teacher; both quote the maxim of Joshua ben Perachiah, choose thyself a master and get thyself a colleague, and Gill adds the rabbinic tradition that made that teacher the master of Jesus of Nazareth. The order is simply inverted here: the choosing was done first and from the other side.

Barnes presses the word itself, which is the one from which election derives, and takes it of their appointment as apostles. The point he draws is the disinterestedness of the love, since it began when they had no affection to offer in return, laid no obligation on the chooser, and therefore binds them the more; and he notes that what the older articles of religion called grace preventing a man means exactly this, grace going before him. Calvin makes the same contrast bear more weight. Men commonly imagine some concurrence between grace and the human will, but the clause claims for Christ alone what is usually divided between the two, since no one is moved of his own accord to seek him until he has been sought. Calvin grants the immediate subject is the special calling to the apostolic office rather than the adoption common to all believers, and then argues from the lesser to the greater: if the office was unmerited, much more is the sonship.

On the second verb the commentators agree the English has drifted. Ellicott warns that ordained has acquired a modern sense that misleads here and would read appointed. Clarke prefers I have placed you, and reports the observation, which he takes from Wetstein, that Theodore of Mopsuestia treated the verb as meaning planted, so that the figure of the vine is still running: not merely planted, but caused to spread through the habitable world. Robertson counts three present subjunctives in the purpose clause and makes them all insist on continuance, a going that keeps going and a fruit that keeps coming, not a spurt.

What the appointment is for is stated plainly enough. Wesley takes the going as conversion of sinners and the abiding fruit as lasting to the end of the world and beyond it, and reads the promise about prayer as a consequence of the going rather than a separate gift. Robertson connects the same promise to the earlier one made in his name. Calvin uses the whole as a spur, since the ground of the exhortation is an undeserved favour, and a favour of that kind obliges diligence rather than excusing it.

The closing verse returns to where the section began, and Ellicott is careful about how. These things means what has gone before, not what follows, and the common mistake of reading it as introducing the command flattens the sense: the precepts were given in order that they might love one another. Gill counts it the third time love has been urged in these last discourses, and thinks the repetition natural after such professions of affection. Augustine takes the command as identifying the fruit: love is the fruit that was spoken of, which is why the apostle names love first among the fruits of the Spirit and treats the rest as springing from it, so that without it nothing profits and with it nothing is lacking to make a man good. Calvin narrows the application to ministers, who are commanded mutual love above all things because without it each labours apart, and what rises is a heap rather than a building. Robertson supplies the reason the command was needed that night, since the men hearing it had been quarrelling about precedence a few hours before.
18:
Ellicott marks the contrast between the love of the previous verse and the hatred of this, and takes the opening verb as imperative, know that it hated me, so the hatred itself becomes a bond with their Master. Robertson treats the condition as assumed true, and notes the perfect tense, has hated and hates still. Calvin explains the warning as a precaution against raw recruits, valiant before they see an enemy and trembling once battle opens, and states the reason flatly: the gospel cannot be published without driving the world to rage. Henry makes hatred the genius of the devil's kingdom as love is of Christ's, and Gill reads the opening clause as granting the fact rather than supposing it.

Who is meant by the world Henry answers in three ways. Their number, since a world of people opposed Christ, with the dry remark that if it were put to a vote between Christ and Satan he fears Satan would out-poll us. Their combination, since Jews and Gentiles who agreed in nothing else agreed in persecuting Christ's ministers. And their spirit, men wholly given to this world and never thinking of another. Clarke passes on a suggestion of Lardner that the first word in the clause is a noun, so that the sense would run, know that it hated me, your Chief.

Why the hatred falls is put several ways. Ellicott finds the selfishness of the world's affection exposed, since it would love not them but whatever in them was its own. Calvin makes the separation itself the cause, adding that they were once part of that world and are distinguished only by mercy, and that none of this contradicts the apostolic rule about living peaceably with all men so far as we can. Barnes turns it into a test, that a man may reckon the enmity of wicked men one evidence of his piety. Robertson turns the test on the reader: does the world hate us, and if not, has the world grown more Christian or Christians more worldly? Clarke quotes a couplet of Gambold that the laws of Christ condemn a vicious world and goad it to revenge, and Wesley reduces it to the plain reason that the maxims, tempers and actions are opposite.

Over the remembered saying two of them differ outright. Ellicott holds the English version exact, the two clauses being necessarily joined because the word of Christ is the word of his disciples, so the world will treat the one as it treated the other. Clarke prefers a different sense for the verb, that they watched his sayings with intent to accuse, and will watch theirs likewise, which he thinks far more agreeable to the context. Calvin reads the first verb as imperative rather than indicative and takes the argument to be that the servant's lot cannot be better than the master's, then notes how it passes from persons to doctrine, nothing troubling the godly more than to see the teaching of God despised. Robertson puts that in a sentence, that the world praises the word of Jesus and dreads to follow it. Augustine notices something the others pass over: in calling them servants here, so soon after saying he would call them servants no longer, the same speaker uses the word he had just withdrawn.

All of them trace the persecution finally to ignorance. Calvin says no one would knowingly fight God, so blindness hurries the world along. Ellicott observes that Acts and the Epistles are one long commentary on the verse. Wesley extends it to all ages and nations. Clarke draws a conclusion none of the others reach: since persecution rests on ignorance of God, those guilty of it, in church or state, know nothing of him; where a worship troubles nobody's peace, no man has the least right to meddle with it, and whoever does is fighting God.
22:
All agree the sin in question is a particular one. Augustine says it is not every sin but one great sin containing the rest and alone blocking forgiveness of the others, unbelief, so that the coming which saved the believing ruined the unbelieving. Lightfoot says the same briefly, that the sin meant is rejecting the Messiah, and refers forward to the next chapter's definition. Ellicott puts it as a change of category: apart from the revelation their fault would have belonged to the times of ignorance God overlooked, the negative evil of men who do not know, whereas now it is the positive evil of men who know and refuse. Barnes adds that the proof offered was argument as much as miracle, and Gill lists the marks of authority that came with the speaking.

On the loss of excuse the language is examined. Clarke renders it without excuse and observes that sin and consequence continue wherever the rejection does. Robertson notes the word means a mere pretence and appears in John only here and two verses later. Calvin anticipates the objection that ignorance might excuse them, answering that the blindness is itself malicious, like a man shutting his eyes against the light, and that the Teacher did his duty without success because their malice would not let them be taught.

Augustine then raises a difficulty nobody else sees. If they are said to hate the Father, yet to act as they do because they do not know him, how can a man hate what he does not know? Either what they hate is something they have imagined, and then it is not God they hate, or they conceive him as he is, and then they cannot be said not to know him. Ellicott traces the ascent instead, from hatred of the disciples to hatred of the Son they represent and of the Father he represents, ending where it must, that a heart able to hate love has hardened past being loved. Gill traces it to the enmity natural to an unregenerate heart and draws comfort from the company the disciples keep in being hated. Wesley makes hatred of God as inseparable from unbelief as love of God is from faith.

The works that none other did raise an objection, answered two ways. Calvin reports the complaint that these miracles were neither more nor greater than those of Moses and the prophets, gives the familiar reply that Christ was not their minister but their author, then widens the word to cover every testimony of divine power in him. Augustine takes a stranger route: granting that prophets raised the dead, he says none healed so many infirmities, and presses the preposition, which means not among them but within them, adding that where earlier men did such works God worked through them, whereas here the power is his own. Barnes sorts the superiority into number, kind, and the fact that prophets invoked a power this speaker simply used. Ellicott notes how the evidence was met, by calling him a sinner with a devil, and concludes that such hearts leave goodness no channel of approach.

The closing quotation is variously placed. Clarke assigns it to the sixty-ninth psalm and treats that psalm as prophetic throughout, mapping its verses onto the abasement, the garden, the crucifixion and what followed. Ellicott thinks the same psalm likeliest while noting the words stand also in the thirty-fifth, and defends without a cause as the true sense of the Hebrew. Robertson allows either and takes law to stand for the whole of Scripture, glossing the adverb as gratuitously and so needlessly. Calvin cites the thirty-fifth and uses it to charge the nation with a malice running unbroken from grandfathers to grandchildren, observing that their law is said not out of respect but to wound, since in it they may see their own manners painted to the life.
26:
Chrysostom frames the paragraph as an answer to an unspoken objection. If men who heard such words and saw such works were not convinced but hated both the Son and the Father, what hope have envoys of being believed? The reply is that another witness is coming. Augustine sharpens it: seeing him they hated and killed him, yet the Advocate will testify so that men believe without seeing; the disciples do not yet speak boldly because they lack the fulness of the Spirit, who will take fear from his friends and turn the hatred of his enemies into love.

Henry makes the largest claim about the verse, that it tells us more of the Holy Spirit than any other single verse in the Bible, and insists the language describes a distinct person rather than a quality or property. He adds that when Christ was reviled he committed his cause to his Father and lost nothing by silence, since the Advocate came and pleaded it powerfully. Wesley argues the same conclusion from the grammar, that coming, being sent, and testifying are personal acts which distinguish the Spirit from both Father and Son, and that the title and the procession can belong to none but a divine person.

How the sending relates to the proceeding is handled carefully. Ellicott notes the emphatic pronoun and treats three descriptions as one act, the mission by the Father at the Son's asking, in the Son's name, and by the Son himself; the clause about proceeding from the Father lends the witness the Father's own weight. Robertson calls the verse the Procession of the Spirit from the Father and from the Son, and observes that the neuter relative should be rendered who, and that the pronoun following is emphatic and masculine though its antecedent is neuter. Wesley reaches the same double procession by argument rather than grammar, from the Spirit being called the Spirit of Christ and from his being sent by the Son.

What the Advocate does Gill sets out most fully: pleading against the world, reproving it of sin and righteousness and judgment, assisting the disciples before princes, and comforting them by applying the things of Christ, shedding abroad the love of God, applying the promises, witnessing their adoption and sealing them. Calvin turns to the effect on the hearer, that a truth sealed by the Spirit on the heart can despise whatever the world raises against it, whereas a faith resting on the opinions of men would be overwhelmed a hundred times a day. Clarke reads the promise as the last step in an argument about inexcusable unbelief: the doctrine was pure, the mission confirmed by miracles, and one thing only remained, to send the Spirit who would convince them.

The apostolic witness Henry calls subordinate to the Spirit's, and the others fill in what it amounted to. Ellicott points out that the tense is present, so they already are witnesses, and that the apostles distinguished their own testimony from the Spirit's; the beginning means the beginning of the Messianic work they had watched. Barnes puts the qualification plainly, that more than three years of observation fitted them to speak of his character and doctrine. Clarke lists the means by which they did it, their miracles, preaching, writings, lives and deaths. Calvin insists the gift was not for their private benefit but for wide diffusion, since they were organs of the Spirit, and uses the pairing against two errors at once, those who think faith is produced by preaching alone and the fanatics who despise outward preaching and talk loftily of secret inspirations; the two are joined here, as in the prophet whose promise sets the Spirit and the words in the mouth together. Robertson ends with a rebuke, that this is the point at which Christians fail most.
